s.dp: Sensory Events and States › Pain, Suffering
s.d: to be in severe or great pain
s.g: to suffer greatly; to be in great pain
s.c: In a number of languages ‘the fire’ must be more clearly marked as the causative agent, so that this expression in ⟦Luke 16:24|Luke 16:24⟧ may be restructured as ‘this fire is causing me great pain.’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Worry, Anxiety, Distress, Peace
s.d: (derivative of {L:ὀδύνη<SDBG:ὀδύνη:000000>} ‘great distress,’ {D:25.235}) to experience great distress or anxiety
s.g: to be very much distressed; to be terribly worried

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Worry, Anxiety, Distress, Peace
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of ὀδύνη ‘physical pain,’ not occurring in the NT) a state of severe emotional anxiety and distress
ritualized wailing and crying as an expression of grief and sorrow at funerals{N:001}

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a Hebrew king in the genealogy of Jesus ({S:04000100800030})
to cause a foul-smelling odor
s.g: to stink; to have a bad smell

s.dp: Spacial Extensions › Extension From a Source
s.d: extension from a source to which the element ὁ refers{N:001}
s.g: from where; from there; from which

s.d: a marker of cause or reason, with focus upon the source{N:002}

s.dp: Artifacts › Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
s.d: a large piece of cloth, probably of linen λίνον

s.dp: Artifacts › Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
s.d: a piece of linen cloth
s.c: In the NT ὀθόνιον occurs only in reference to strips of cloth used in preparing a corpse for burial.

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Groups and Members of Groups of Persons Regarded as Related by Blood but without Special Reference to Successive Generations
s.d: (derivative of {L:οἶκος<SDBG:οἶκος:000001>}[b] ‘family,’ {D:10.8}) one who belongs to a particular household or extended family
the group of servants working in a particular household
a servant in a household
s.g: house servant; household servant; personal servant

s.d: to live or dwell in a place
to remain in a place defined psychologically or spiritually
s.g: to be in; to live in; to dwell in; to reside in

s.dp: Constructions › Parts and Areas of Buildings
s.d: a room or quarters where one may stay (normally a part of a house)
s.c: In ⟦Acts 12:7|Acts 12:7⟧ οἴκημα is used to refer to a prison cell, and in this context it is best translated as ‘room’ or ‘room in the prison.’

s.d: (derivative of {L:οἰκέω<SDBG:οἰκέω:000000>}[a] ‘to dwell,’ {D:85.67}) a place in which one may dwell
a building or place where one dwells
s.c: The size of an οἰκία or of an οἶκος (LN 7.2) may differ greatly. For example, the house referred to in ⟦Luke 7:10|Luke 7:10⟧ would no doubt have been relatively elaborate, and in ⟦Matthew 11:8|Matthew 11:8⟧ οἶκος refers to the palace in which Herod lived. In a number of languages it is important to distinguish clearly between various types of dwellings depending upon their size and presumed importance. Accordingly, in rendering οἰκία or οἶκος it is necessary to use a number of different terms roughly equivalent to the English series ‘cottage,’ ‘house,’ ‘official residence,’ ‘palace,’ ‘temple,’ etc.|In a number of languages one must distinguish carefully between a house and a home. A term meaning ‘house’ would be used in referring to any dwelling as a construction, while a term meaning ‘home’ would be used in referring to the more or less permanent dwelling of a particular person. In ⟦Mark 2:1|Mark 2:1⟧, for example, it is significant to indicate that Jesus was dwelling in the house through the roof of which the paralyzed man was let down.

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Groups and Members of Groups of Persons Regarded as Related by Blood but without Special Reference to Successive Generations
s.d: the family consisting of those related by blood and marriage, as well as slaves and servants, living in the same house or homestead
s.c: In a number of languages the equivalent of οἶκος or οἰκία would be ‘those who live together’ or ‘those who have the same fence’ (this being a reference to a group of huts surrounded by a fence and thus constituting a single so-called ‘family unit’).

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Have, Possess, Property, Owner
s.d: (figurative extension of meaning of {L:οἰκία<SDBG:οἰκία:000000>}[a] ‘house,’ {D:7.3}) possessions associated with a house and household
s.c: It is also possible in ⟦Mark 12:40|Mark 12:40⟧ to understand τὰς οἰκίας as meaning specifically ‘houses.’

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Groups and Members of Groups of Persons Regarded as Related by Blood but without Special Reference to Successive Generations
s.d: (derivative of {L:οἶκος<SDBG:οἶκος:000001>}[b] ‘family,’ {D:10.8}) one who belongs to a particular household or extended family
to command and give leadership to a household{N:001}
s.g: to direct a household; to manage a home

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Have, Possess, Property, Owner
s.d: one who owns and manages a household, including family, servants, and slaves
to make or erect any kind of construction{N:001}
to increase the potential of someone or something, with focus upon the process involved
s.g: to strengthen; to make more able; to build up

s.d: (derivative of {L:οἰκοδομέω<SDBG:οἰκοδομέω:000000>}[a] ‘to build,’ {D:45.1}) one who builds
s.c: Normally refers to builders of houses and other types of relatively large constructions.

s.d: any type of building or structure which encloses an area, but the area may be open to the sky, as in the case of amphitheaters{N:001}
the construction of something, with focus on the event of building up or on the result of such an event
s.g: to build up; to construct; construction
s.c: In ⟦1 Corinthians 3:9|1 Corinthians 3:9⟧ the phrase θεοῦ οἰκοδομή has been interpreted by many as ‘a dwelling place for God’ (see LN 7.1), but it is more likely that the Christian is regarded as the result of God’s activity, that is to say, the believer is ‘God’s construction’ or ‘that which God has made.’ οἰκοδομή in ⟦2 Corinthians 5:1|2 Corinthians 5:1⟧ (οἰκοδομὴν ἐκ θεοῦ ἔχομεν ‘we have a construction from God’) may be regarded as having essentially the same meaning as in ⟦1 Corinthians 3:9|1 Corinthians 3:9⟧, though the reference here is to the glorified body.

s.d: to increase the potential of someone or something, with focus upon the process involved
s.g: to strengthen; to make more able; to build up

s.d: to manage and provide for a household
s.g: to manage a household; to run a household; to be in charge of a household
s.c: In biblical times a household would consist of more than the nuclear family, that is to say, more than simply husband, wife, and children, for servants, slaves, and permanent hired workers living with the family would be regarded as a part of the total household.

s.d: a task involving management and organization

s.dp: Think › To Intend, To Purpose, To Plan
s.d: a plan which involves a set of arrangements (referring in the NT to God’s plan for bringing salvation to mankind within the course of history)
to manage and provide for a household
s.g: to manage a household; to run a household; to be in charge of a household
s.c: In biblical times a household would consist of more than the nuclear family, that is to say, more than simply husband, wife, and children, for servants, slaves, and permanent hired workers living with the family would be regarded as a part of the total household.

s.d: one who is in charge of running a household
s.c: It may be necessary in some languages to indicate that οἰκονόμος was a person hired to engage in a particular activity, and therefore in ⟦Luke 16:1|Luke 16:1⟧ it may be necessary to say ‘there was a rich man who had hired a man to manage his household.’

s.d: one who has the authority and responsibility for something
s.g: one who is in charge of; one who is responsible for; adminstrator; manager

s.d: (an idiom, literally: manager of a city) one who is in charge of the finances of a city

a building consisting of one or more rooms and normally serving as a dwelling place (οἶκος[a] also includes certain public buildings, for example, a temple. The extension of οἶκος[a] to include temples may be the result of speaking of a temple as the dwelling place of the deity.)
s.c: For a discussion of certain translational problems related to οἶκος, see LN 7.3.

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Groups and Members of Groups of Persons Regarded as Related by Blood but without Special Reference to Successive Generations
s.d: the family consisting of those related by blood and marriage, as well as slaves and servants, living in the same house or homestead
s.c: In a number of languages the equivalent of οἶκος or οἰκία would be ‘those who live together’ or ‘those who have the same fence’ (this being a reference to a group of huts surrounded by a fence and thus constituting a single so-called ‘family unit’).|In ⟦Acts 7:10|Acts 7:10⟧ οἶκος can mean the household over which Joseph was placed, or it can mean the property of Pharaoh (see LN 57.21).

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Kinship Relations Involving Successive Generations
s.d: persons of successive generations who are related by birth
s.c: In biblical times the reckoning of a lineage was somewhat complex in view of certain distinctions between legal and biological relations. The focus of meaning in γένεσις, οἶκος, and πατριά is not, however, the list of ancestors, but the lineage of successively related persons to which the reference person belongs. Some scholars, however, interpret γένεσις history, LN 33.19).|In some languages a successive series of ancestors is called ‘the forefathers’ or ‘those to whom one looks back’ or ‘those who have gone ahead.’ In other languages a lineage is referred to as ‘a person’s root’ or ‘a man’s trunk’ (referring to the trunk of a tree).|In ⟦Luke 2:4|Luke 2:4⟧ there appears to be no significant difference in meaning between οἶκος and πατριά, and in some receptor languages it would be sufficient to use a single term essentially equivalent to ‘lineage.’ The two terms appear to simply reinforce their shared meaning.

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Have, Possess, Property, Owner
s.d: (figurative extension of meaning of {L:οἶκος<SDBG:οἶκος:000000>}[a] ‘house,’ {D:7.2}) possessions associated with a house and household
s.c: The rendering ‘property’ seems to be far more justified by the context and by general usage than the more common meaning of ‘household’ (see LN 10.8).

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Political
s.d: (idioms, literally: house of Israel, and: house of Judah, respectively) the people of Israel as an ethnic entity
s.g: the people of Israel; the nation of Israel
s.c: In translating the expression ‘the people of Israel’ it may be necessary to use an appositional phrase, for example, ‘the people, namely, Israel’ or a relative clause which also serves an appositional function, for example, ‘the people who are Israel.’ In some languages it may be preferable to use a term such as ‘nation’ followed by some expression which will indicate that Israel is simply the name of the nation, for example, ‘the nation called Israel.’

s.d: a building consisting of one or more rooms and serving as a place of worship
a building consisting of one or more rooms and serving as a dwelling place

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › The Earth's Surface
s.d: the surface of the earth as the dwelling place of mankind, in contrast with the heavens above and the world below{N:001}
s.c: In ⟦Hebrews 2:5|Hebrews 2:5⟧ there is a reference to τὴν οἰκουμένην τὴν μέλλουσαν ‘the world to come, the future world.’ This has generally been interpreted as being equivalent to ‘the coming age,’ but the use of οἰκουμένη would seem to imply an inhabited world.

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Governmental Administrative Areas
s.d: the Roman Empire, including its inhabitants (οἰκουμένη[b] differs from {L:οἰκουμένη<SDBG:οἰκουμένη:000000>}[a] ‘earth,’ {D:1.39}, in that those outside of the Roman Empire are specifically excluded, that is to say, no census was to be taken of the barbarians, but only of the inhabitants of the Empire)
s.c: In order to represent accurately the meaning of οἰκουμένη in ⟦Luke 2:1|Luke 2:1⟧ it may be possible to translate ‘Emperor Augustus sent out an order that all the people over whom he ruled should register themselves for the census.’

s.d: (figurative extension of meaning of {L:οἰκουμένη<SDBG:οἰκουμένη:000000>}[a] ‘inhabited earth,’ {D:1.39}) all people who dwell on the earth
one who works in the home
s.g: one who takes care of the home; homemaker

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Mercy, Merciless
s.d: to show mercy and concern, with the implication of sensitivity and compassion
s.g: to have mercy; to show compassion; mercy; tender compassion

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Mercy, Merciless
s.d: (derivative of {L:οἰκτίρω<SDBG:οἰκτίρω:000000>} ‘to have mercy,’ {D:88.80}) pertaining to showing mercy or compassion
s.c: In a number of languages expressions involving showing mercy or being merciful are expressed in highly idiomatic ways, for example, ‘to show one’s heart toward,’ ‘to feel in one’s stomach for,’ ‘to have one’s heart go out toward,’ or ‘to treat as a loving child.’

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Mercy, Merciless
s.d: to show mercy and concern, with the implication of sensitivity and compassion
s.g: to have mercy; to show compassion; mercy; tender compassion

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Drunkenness
s.d: a person who habitually drinks too much and thus becomes a drunkard{N:001}
a fermented beverage made from the juice of grapes{N:001}
s.c: Though some persons have argued that whenever mention is made of Jesus either making or drinking wine, one must assume that this was only unfermented grape juice, there is no real basis for such a conclusion. Only where οἶνος νέος ‘new wine’ (LN 6.198) is mentioned can one assume that this is unfermented grape juice or grape juice in the initial stages of fermentation.|In a number of languages there is no indigenous term for wine, and some expression may simply be borrowed from a dominant language. On the other hand, it is sometimes possible to employ a descriptive phrase, for example, ‘fermented fruit juice.’ In some languages the equivalent for ‘wine’ is more specifically ‘palm wine,’ that is to say, a wine made from the sap of certain palm trees. Such a term may also have a more generic meaning and be applicable to any kind of wine.|There are a number of passages in the NT where one must be particularly careful in the selection of terms to translate wine. For example, in ⟦Ephesians 5:18|Ephesians 5:18⟧ a literal translation of ‘do not get drunk with wine’ could be interpreted to mean that it is permissible for one to get drunk on other types of intoxicating liquors. It may, therefore, be necessary in some languages to render ⟦Ephesians 5:18|Ephesians 5:18⟧ as simply ‘do not get drunk.’|In ⟦Luke 10:34|Luke 10:34⟧ (κατέδησεν τὰ τραύματα αὐτοῦ ἐπιχέων ἔλαιον καὶ οἶνον ‘he poured on olive oil and wine and bandaged his wounds’) it is important to recognize the medicinal value of oil and wine. In some instances translators have indicated the purpose of such an activity by translating ‘to cleanse and heal his wounds he poured wine and oil on them and bandaged them.’ It may also be possible to add in a marginal note information as to the antiseptic quality of the wine and the value of the oil in the healing process.

s.d: a set phrase referring to newly pressed grape juice, unfermented or in the initial stages of fermentation
a set phrase referring to wine drugged with myrrh and used as a stupefying potion{N:003}
s.c: In general, ἐσμυρνισμένος οἶνος must be rendered by means of a phrase or a clause, for example, ‘wine which has been mixed with a drug called myrrh’ or ‘wine mixed with a drug to reduce pain.’ It is, of course, also possible to use an abbreviated phrase such as ‘myrrhed wine’ and then to place the explanation of its function in a marginal note.

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Drunkenness
s.d: drunkenness, implying the consumption of a large quantity of wine

s.dp: Hold a View, Believe, Trust › Suppose, Think Possible
s.d: to regard something as presumably true, but without particular certainty
s.g: to suppose; to presume; to assume; to imagine; to believe; to think
s.c: In some languages the equivalent of ‘to suppose’ or ‘to presume’ is ‘to think somewhat’ or ‘to think perhaps’ or ‘to think a little.’ In some instances the lack of certainty is spelled out clearly as ‘to think, but not with certainty’ or ‘to think, but not to know’ or ‘to think, but not to be sure.’

s.d: pertaining to being similar to something else in some respect{N:001}
interrogative references to class or kind
s.g: what sort of; what kind of
s.c: This meaning is also found as a variant reading: ὑγιὴς ἐγίνετο οἵῳ δήποτ οὖν κατείχετο νοσήματι ‘was made well from whatever disease he had’ ⟦John 5:3|John 5:3⟧ (apparatus).

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
s.d: to extend a period of time, with the implication of lack of activity

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Laziness, Idleness
s.d: pertaining to shrinking from or hesitating to engage in something worthwhile, possibly implying lack of ambition

s.dp: Trouble, Hardship, Relief, Favorable Circumstances › Trouble, Hardship, Distress
s.d: pertaining to being bothersome
s.g: bothersome; to be a bother to not mind (in combination with οὐκ)

s.dp: Time › Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
s.d: pertaining to taking place on the eighth in a series of days
s.c: Since in NT times the counting of days involved numbering both the first and the last day in a series, ὀκταήμερος may be rendered as ‘a week later’ or ‘seven days later.’ Compare ἡμέραι ὀκτώ ‘eight days’ (⟦Luke 2:21|Luke 2:21⟧) as being equivalent to one week; see discussion at LN 60.17.

s.d: cardinal number, where there are eight instances of a countable entity
s.c: To designate a week, the normal practice in NT times was to speak of ‘eight days,’ since in a series both the first and the last days were counted. The equivalent in many languages would be simply ‘after seven days had passed’ (⟦Luke 2:21|Luke 2:21⟧).

s.d: a state of utter ruin or destruction{N:001}
to cause the complete destruction or ruin of someone or something{N:002}

s.dp: Hold a View, Believe, Trust › Trust, Rely
s.d: pertaining to having relatively little faith
s.g: of little faith; of insufficient faith

s.d: a relatively small quantity on any dimension
a relatively low point on a scale of extent
s.g: little; to a small degree; slight
s.c: The first ὀλίγον in ⟦Luke 7:47|Luke 7:47⟧ is an expression of quantity (see LN 59.13), while the second ὀλίγον indicates degree. Accordingly, in some languages it may be necessary to translate ⟦Luke 7:47|Luke 7:47⟧ as ‘but whoever has been forgiven only a few things loves only a little bit.’|In a number of languages, however, it is impossible to speak of ‘not a little’ (a case of litotes or purposeful understatement). The appropriate equivalent in ⟦Acts 12:18|Acts 12:18⟧ would be simply ‘there was great confusion among the guards’ or ‘the guards were intensely disturbed’ or ‘the guards were in tremendous confusion.’

s.d: a relatively small quantity

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: pertaining to a relatively brief extent of time{N:001}
s.g: a little while; for a little while; a short time; brief; briefly
s.c: It is also possible to interpret ἐν ὀλίγῳ in ⟦Acts 26:28|Acts 26:28⟧ as meaning ‘easily’ or ‘without difficulty’ (see LN 22.41).|In some languages it may be best to translate the phrase in ⟦1 Peter 5:12|1 Peter 5:12⟧ as ‘I have written a brief letter.’

s.d: pertaining to having limited or diminished motivation for the attainment of some goal
s.c: The expression ‘those who are losing heart’ (⟦1 Thessalonians 5:14|1 Thessalonians 5:14⟧) is semantically negative, but can be expressed in a more specifically negative form in some languages, for example, ‘those who do not have courage’ or ‘those whose hearts are not strong.’

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Despise, Scorn, Contempt
s.d: to regard something or someone as of little value
s.g: to look down on; to have contempt for; to make light of; to despise

s.d: (derivative of {L:ὀλοθρεύω<SDBG:ὀλοθρεύω:000000>} ‘to destroy, to ruin,’ {D:20.34}) one who causes destruction
s.c: In ⟦1 Corinthians 10:10|1 Corinthians 10:10⟧ ὀλοθρευτής may serve as a title referring to a destroying angel or even to Satan.

s.d: to cause the complete destruction or ruin of someone or something{N:001}
an animal which has been sacrificed to God and completely burned up on the altar

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Health, Vigor, Strength
s.d: a state of complete health or soundness in all parts of the body
s.c: In some languages it may be possible to translate ὁλοκληρίαν as ‘very healthy’ or ‘all parts of his body are healthy’ or ‘… strong.’

s.d: a totality, with special emphasis upon the entity as a whole
s.c: In a number of languages it may be difficult to speak of ‘your entire being.’ A substitute expression in ⟦1 Thessalonians 5:23|1 Thessalonians 5:23⟧ may be ‘yourselves as one person.’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Laugh, Cry, Groan
s.d: to make a loud cry as an expression of either joy or sorrow
s.g: to make a loud cry; to cry aloud
s.c: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘cry aloud’ would simply be ‘scream.’ In this one occurrence of ὀλολύζω in the NT, the context refers to desperate circumstances, and one must often select an expression for ‘screaming’ or ‘crying’ which will be in keeping with this context referring to the threat of future misery.

s.d: pertaining to being whole, complete, or entire, with focus on unity
a totality as a complete unit
a degree of totality or completeness{N:001}
a degree of completeness, with the possible implication of purpose or result

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a person greeted in {S:04501601500022}
fruit of the fig tree συκῆ, produced late in the summer season (and often falling off before it ripens)
s.c: In the only context in which ὄλυνθος occurs in the NT (⟦Revelation 6:13|Revelation 6:13⟧), one may employ an expression such as ‘unripe fig’ or ‘fig which ripens late.’

s.d: a degree of totality or completeness{N:001}
s.c: In ⟦Matthew 5:34|Matthew 5:34⟧ ὅλως should not be interpreted as a qualifier of ὀμόσαι ‘to swear,’ for this is not a matter of ‘not swearing completely,’ but ὅλως is a degree attributive of the proposition ‘do not swear.’ In a number of languages the closest equivalent is ‘do not ever swear’ or ‘under no circumstances whatsoever make an oath.’

s.d: pertaining to reality, with the implication of being generally known{N:002}

a heavy rain, either in length of occurrence or in force, as in the case of a thunderstorm (thus differing from {L:ὑετός<SDBG:ὑετός:000001>}[b], {L:βροχή<SDBG:βροχή:000000>} and {L:βρέχω<SDBG:βρέχω:000000>}[a] in {D:14.10})
s.c: In some languages a rainstorm is simply ‘a rain with wind,’ but it may also be expressed as ‘rain that hurts’ or ‘rain that floods.’

s.d: to speak with someone, with the implication of a reversal of roles in communication
to associate with one another, normally involving spacial proximity and/or joint activity, and usually implying some kind of reciprocal relation or involvement
s.g: to associate; to be in the company of; to be involved with; association
s.c: In translating terms referring to association, one may employ a number of different kinds of expressions, for example, ‘to have something to do with,’ ‘to keep company with,’ ‘to go around with,’ ‘to join in doing things together,’ or ‘to become a companion of.’ Sometimes association is spoken of in terms of the impression made upon others, for example, ‘to be seen often together,’ ‘to be regarded as close friends,’ and even idiomatically as ‘to be another person’s shadow.’

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
s.d: the organ of sight in humans and many animals, occurring in a pair in the face or elsewhere on the head
s.c: In a number of languages an important distinction is made between the eyes consisting of the eyeballs and the eyes covered or partially covered by the eyelids. In ⟦Matthew 9:29|Matthew 9:29⟧ and ⟦Matthew 20:34|Matthew 20:34⟧, Jesus apparently touched the eyelids, not the eyeballs.

s.dp: Communication › Swear, Put Under Oath, Vow
s.d: to affirm the truth of a statement by calling on a divine being to execute sanctions against a person if the statement in question is not true (in the case of a deity taking an oath, his divine being is regarded as validating the statement)
s.g: to swear; to make an oath; oath
s.c: In a number of languages it is necessary to be quite specific in referring to the swearing of an oath, for example, ‘to say something by calling upon God to listen’ or ‘to state that something is true and asking God to punish if it is not true’ or ‘to make God responsible for what one has said.’|For ⟦Mark 14:71|Mark 14:71⟧ see LN 33.472.

s.dp: Hold a View, Believe, Trust › Agree, Consent
s.d: pertaining to mutual consent or agreement
s.g: with one mind; by common consent; unanimously
s.c: In a number of languages with one mind (⟦Acts 1:14|Acts 1:14⟧) would need to be rendered as ‘prayed for the same things’ or ‘said the same in their prayers.’|In ⟦Acts 15:25|Acts 15:25⟧ the expression ‘we unanimously agreed’ may also be rendered as ‘we were in agreement that.’

s.d: pertaining to having the same kinds of feelings or desires
s.g: same kinds of feelings; same kinds of desires

s.d: pertaining to being similar to something else in some respect{N:001}
the state of being similar to something
to be like or similar to something else
s.g: to be like; to resemble; to be similar to

s.d: to consider something to be like something else{N:001}
the state of being similar to something
pertaining to being similar to something else in some respect{N:001}
the state of being similar to something
to express openly one’s allegiance to a proposition or person
s.c: It is often extremely difficult, if not impossible, to translate ὁμολογέω, ὁμολογία, and ἐξομολογέω by the usual expression for ‘confess,’ since this would usually imply that one has done something wrong. It is normally necessary, therefore, to employ quite a different type of relationship, usually involving a public utterance and an expression of confidence or allegiance. For example, in ⟦Matthew 10:32|Matthew 10:32⟧ it may be necessary to translate ‘whoever tells people publicly that he is loyal to me, I will tell my Father that I am loyal to that person.’ Similarly, in ⟦Hebrews 10:23|Hebrews 10:23⟧ one may translate ‘let us hold on to the hope in which we have told people we have such confidence.’ Likewise, in ⟦Romans 15:9|Romans 15:9⟧ one may translate ‘therefore I will tell the Gentiles how I have put my confidence in you.’

s.d: to acknowledge a fact publicly, often in reference to previous bad behavior
s.c: In ⟦Philippians 2:11|Philippians 2:11⟧ the statement πᾶσα γλῶσσα ἐξομολογήσηται ὅτι κύριος Ἰησοῦς Χριστός (‘that everyone may confess that Jesus Christ is Lord’) means simply to acknowledge a fact publicly, and in this instance there is no implication of previous bad behavior.

s.d: to make an emphatic declaration, often public, and at times in response to pressure or an accusation
act of expressing openly one’s allegiance to a proposition or person
s.c: It is often extremely difficult, if not impossible, to translate ὁμολογέω, ὁμολογία, and ἐξομολογέω by the usual expression for ‘confess,’ since this would usually imply that one has done something wrong. It is normally necessary, therefore, to employ quite a different type of relationship, usually involving a public utterance and an expression of confidence or allegiance. For example, in ⟦Matthew 10:32|Matthew 10:32⟧ it may be necessary to translate ‘whoever tells people publicly that he is loyal to me, I will tell my Father that I am loyal to that person.’ Similarly, in ⟦Hebrews 10:23|Hebrews 10:23⟧ one may translate ‘let us hold on to the hope in which we have told people we have such confidence.’ Likewise, in ⟦Romans 15:9|Romans 15:9⟧ one may translate ‘therefore I will tell the Gentiles how I have put my confidence in you.’

s.d: (derivative of {L:ὁμολογέω<SDBG:ὁμολογέω:000001>}[b] ‘to admit,’ {D:33.275}) pertaining to what must or should be admitted or acknowledged publicly
s.g: admittedly; to be admitted; one must admit

s.d: pertaining to joint activity in some occupation or craft
s.g: of the same trade; of the same craft; involved in the same occupation; having the same kind of work

s.d: a marker of association, based on similarity of activity or state
pertaining to being of the same mind or having the same thoughts as someone else
s.c: In some languages it may be better to speak of ‘having the same attitudes’ or, idiomatically, ‘having thoughts that follow the same path.’

s.d: a marker of concession, with the possible implication of an added aspect of similarity
s.c: The interpretation of ὅμως in ⟦Galatians 3:15|Galatians 3:15⟧ and ⟦1 Corinthians 14:7|1 Corinthians 14:7⟧ as indicating concession is doubtful, and it may be preferable to understand ὅμως in these contexts as meaning ‘likewise’ or ‘similarly,’ for example, ‘similarly, in the case of a human will, no one annuls it’ and ‘similarly, in the case of a flute or harp, lifeless instruments which produce a sound’ (see LN 64.11).

s.d: pertaining to being, at least in some respects, similar
s.c: For another interpretation of ὅμως in ⟦Galatians 3:15|Galatians 3:15⟧, see LN 89.74.

s.d: a marker of an implied clause of concession{N:001}
a dream as a means of communication{N:001}
s.c: In a number of languages there are different terms for ‘dream’ depending upon the nature of the dream. A frightening dream without special significance or a dream with erotic implications may be referred to by terms which are quite different from a term referring to a dream which carries important meaning, in other words, a dream which constitutes a type of vision or symbol of some reality.

s.d: the young of a donkey ὄνος
s.c: As in the case of ὄνος ‘donkey’ (LN 4.31), a number of languages make a distinction either in form or in terms for the young of a donkey based upon distinctions in sex.

s.d: to speak disparagingly of a person in a manner which is not justified
to reproach someone, with the implication of that individual being evidently to blame
act of speaking disparagingly of a person in a manner which is not justified

s.dp: Status › Low Status or Rank [including persons of low status]
s.d: a low status characterized by public disgrace

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a slave of Philemon

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a Christian mentioned in {S:05500101600012} and {S:05500401900014}
(derivative of {L:ὄνος<SDBG:ὄνος:000000>} ‘donkey,’ {D:4.31}) pertaining to a donkey
s.c: In rendering ⟦Matthew 18:6|Matthew 18:6⟧ it is important to avoid the impression that a donkey would turn the millstone in the same way that a person would. Sometimes a general causative expression may be used, for example, ‘a millstone that a donkey causes to go round (rotate),’ but it may actually be necessary to say ‘… which a donkey causes to go round (rotate) by pulling on a shaft.’ In fact, a marginal note may be necessary in order to avoid serious misunderstanding and to emphasize the fact that such a millstone was large and heavy.

s.d: to be the recipient of help or favor
s.g: to receive help; to receive a benefit; to be favored

s.d: the proper name of a person or object
(a figurative extension of meaning of {L:ὄνομα<SDBG:ὄνομα:000000>}[a] ‘name,’ {D:33.126}) a person, with the possible implication of existence or relevance as individuals{N:001}
s.c: In some instances ἄνθρωπος ‘people’ (LN 9.1) occurs together with ὄνομα without any significant distinction in meaning (e.g. ⟦Revelation 11:13|Revelation 11:13⟧). See also LN 9.20.

s.d: that which is said about a person on the basis of an evaluation of the person’s conduct
s.c: In obtaining a satisfactory equivalent for ‘reputation,’ it may be necessary to restructure considerably the clause in which a term such as μαρτυρία or ὄνομα occurs. For example, in ⟦1 Timothy 3:7|1 Timothy 3:7⟧ one may translate ‘he should be the kind of man that people outside the church say is a good person.’ Similarly, in ⟦Revelation 3:1|Revelation 3:1⟧ one may need to translate ‘people speak of you as being alive even though you are dead.’

s.d: category or kind, based upon an implied designation for a class of entities
s.g: category of; being of the type that

s.d: (an idiom, literally: to name the name of the Lord) to employ the name of the Lord as evidence that one worships the Lord
s.g: to say that one belongs to the Lord or to declare that one is a worshiper of the Lord
in the name of; by/with/on the authority of

s.d: (an idiom, literally: to throw out the name) to insult or slander, with a possible implication of a kind of psychological ostracism
to give a name or title to
s.g: to call; to give a name to; to give a title to

s.d: to utter a name in a ritual context (without directly referring to the person or speaking about the person in question)
s.g: to pronounce a name; to call out a name

s.d: to speak of something by mentioning the name of it
s.c: There may be certain problems involved in translating ὀνομάζω in ⟦Ephesians 5:3|Ephesians 5:3⟧, for the text does not mean that one should never use a term such as πλεονεξία ‘greed’ (LN 25.22). The meaning is simply that there should never be a reason for having to speak about greed, since the people should not themselves be guilty of such behavior.

s.d: (an idiom, literally: to name the name of the Lord) to employ the name of the Lord as evidence that one worships the Lord
s.g: to say that one belongs to the Lord or to declare that one is a worshiper of the Lord

s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:ὀνομάζω<SDBG:ὀνομάζω:000001>}[b] ‘to call a name,’ {D:33.133}) to be caused to be made known
s.c: It would be possible, however, to interpret ὀνομάζομαι in ⟦Romans 15:20|Romans 15:20⟧ in a more literal sense, so that one could translate the final part of the verse as ‘where the name of Christ had not been used’ or ‘where no one had spoken the name of Christ.’

s.d: domestic animal belonging to the same family as the horse, but smaller and with longer ears; it can have variety of colors from dark brown, through light brown to gray and occasionally white; Equus Asinus africanus; used to ride on, carry loads, or do other work
s.c: In the context of ⟦John 12:15|John 12:15⟧ the reference is obviously to a female donkey.|In languages in which there is no word for ‘donkey,’ it is usually best to borrow a term from a dominant language rather than attempting some type of descriptive equivalent. For example, in one language a descriptive designation, namely, ‘a long-eared animal,’ was understood by the people as referring to a rabbit. In some languages donkey is referred to as ‘a kind of small horse’ or ‘a small horse-like animal.’|Though in Greek the article and/or other attributives to the noun ὄνος indicate by their forms whether ὄνος is to be understood as masculine or feminine, in a number of languages quite different terms are employed for a male or female donkey.

s.d: pertaining to actual existence{N:001}
a cheap, sour wine (evidently a favorite beverage of poorer people and relatively effective in quenching thirst)
s.c: ‘Sour wine’ is sometimes rendered as ‘bitter wine’ or ‘sour juice.’

s.d: pertaining to having a thin cutting edge

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: pertaining to a very short period of time, with the probable implication of special haste
s.c: It would also be possible to understand ὀξεῖς οἱ πόδες αὐτῶν ‘their feet are swift’ as being an idiom, but ὀξύς occurs frequently in non-biblical Greek with the meaning of ‘quick, swift, soon.’ In ⟦Romans 3:15|Romans 3:15⟧ οἱ πόδες αὐτῶν is a metonymic expression meaning ‘the people,’ so that it is not simply the feet that are swift to shed blood, but it is the people who are quick to kill.

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Depressions and Holes
s.d: an opening or hole in the ground, either large as in {S:05801103800032} or relatively small as in {S:05900301100014}
s.c: Holes would differ from caves (⟦Hebrews 11:38|Hebrews 11:38⟧) in that holes would be vertical openings into the ground, while caves would be more or less horizontal openings into cliffs or sides of hills. In ⟦James 3:11|James 3:11⟧ it may be quite unnecessary, and in fact confusing, to try to translate ὀπῆς, since ἐκ τῆς αὐτῆς ὀπῆς ‘from the same opening’ would seem to be redundant with ἡ πηγή ‘spring,’ since a spring would presumably only flow from a hole or opening in the ground.

s.dp: Spacial Extensions › Extension From a Source
s.d: extension from a source which is behind

s.dp: Spacial Positions › In Front Of, Face To Face, In Back Of, Behind
s.d: a position on the back surface of an object
s.g: the back of; in back of; on the back of

s.d: the outside surface of an object
s.c: The manner in which ἔξωθεν, ἐκτός, and ὄπισθεν may be rendered in particular contexts depends very largely upon what is being spoken about. For example, ἔξωθεν in ⟦1 Peter 3:3|1 Peter 3:3⟧ refers to the outward aids employed in making oneself beautiful, but instead of speaking of such objects as being on the surface or on the outside, it may be necessary to speak of those things which one puts on the body or what one wears.

s.dp: Spacial Positions › In Front Of, Face To Face, In Back Of, Behind
s.d: a position behind an object or other position

s.dp: Guide, Discipline, Follow › Follow, Be a Disciple
s.d: marker of one who is followed as a leader (occurring with a variety of verbs indicating change of state or movement)

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
s.d: a marker of a point of time closely associated with a prior point of time
(a figurative extension of meaning of ὁπλίζομαι ‘to arm oneself,’ not occurring in the NT) to prepare, with focus upon the process of equipping
any type of tool or instrument
s.c: In ⟦Romans 6:13|Romans 6:13⟧ ὅπλον is generally interpreted as being used figuratively as a reference to parts of the body which may be instruments for doing evil.

s.d: an instrument used in fighting, whether offensive or defensive
s.c: In the NT ὅπλον also occurs in the figurative sense of non-material means of fighting, e.g. ⟦2 Corinthians 6:7|2 Corinthians 6:7⟧.

s.d: interrogative references to class or kind
s.g: what sort of; what kind of

s.d: a reference to a position in space (often used with ἐάν or ἄν ‘ever,’ {D:71.8}, to mark an indefinite and unrestricted position in space)
a relative reference to a set of circumstances
a marker of cause or reason, with special reference to a set of relevant circumstances
a marker of an area of activity which bears some relation to something else
s.g: in; about; in the case of; with regard to
